opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it's a great question. When we started working on this, around 2019, GANs were really the dominant approach for image generation, and they could produce very sharp, impressive samples. But they had some well-known issues. Training is a minimax game between a generator and a discriminator, and that makes it quite unstable. You need a lot of tricks and careful hyperparameter tuning to get it to work, and you often run into problems like mode collapse, where the model only captures part of the data distribution. And you don't really have a principled way of evaluating likelihoods or comparing models.

Autoregressive models, on the other hand, are very stable to train, because it's just maximum likelihood, and they have good coverage of the distribution. But for images you have to impose an arbitrary ordering over the pixels and generate them one at a time, which is slow, and it's not obviously the right inductive bias for spatial data.

What we found exciting about the score-based perspective was that you could sidestep both of those problems. Instead of modeling the probability density directly, which requires dealing with the normalization constant, you model the gradient of the log density, the score function. And it turns out you can learn that with a simple regression-style objective, denoising score matching, which is very stable. No adversarial training, no architectural constraints like you need for normalizing flows.

The key insight was to perturb the data with noise at many different scales. At high noise levels the distribution is smooth and easy to estimate everywhere in space, and as you anneal the noise down, you gradually recover the fine structure of the data. Then you can generate samples by essentially starting from pure noise and iteratively denoising, following the learned scores.

So you get the stability and mode coverage of likelihood-based models, you get sample quality that eventually matched and then surpassed GANs, and you also get a lot of flexibility. Because you have a model of the score, you can do things like controllable generation, inpainting, solving inverse problems, and, through the connection to stochastic differential equations, even compute exact likelihoods. That combination of being principled, stable, and really flexible is what made us believe this was a very promising direction.

r001.rationale: It says GAN training is an unstable minimax game between the generator and discriminator.

r002.rationale: It attributes stability to learning scores with the denoising score matching objective.

r003.rationale: It says sampling starts from pure noise and iteratively denoises using the learned scores.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so to give a bit of context, when we started working on this, around 2019, the landscape of generative modeling was really dominated by two families of approaches. On one side you had GANs, which could produce very high quality samples, but they were notoriously difficult to train. You have this adversarial game between a generator and a discriminator, and the optimization is unstable, you get mode collapse, and you have to be very careful with hyperparameters. And fundamentally, a GAN doesn't give you a likelihood, so it's hard to evaluate and hard to use for things other than sampling.

On the other side you had likelihood-based models, things like autoregressive models and normalizing flows and VAEs. Those are much more principled from a statistical point of view. You're maximizing the likelihood of the data, training is stable, you can compare models. But each of them had its own constraints. Autoregressive models have to generate pixels one at a time, so sampling is very slow for high-resolution images. Flows require invertible architectures, which restricts what you can do. VAEs tend to give you blurry samples.

So the question we were asking ourselves was, is there a way to get the best of both worlds? Something that trains with a simple, stable objective like the likelihood-based models, but produces samples with the quality of a GAN, and doesn't put strong architectural constraints on the network.

And the key idea, which came out of the work Yang Song and I did on score-based generative modeling, was to not model the density directly, but to model the gradient of the log density, what's called the score. The nice thing about the score is that it doesn't need to be normalized, so you're free of the normalizing constant that makes likelihood training so hard, and you can use essentially any neural network architecture you want. You estimate the score at many different noise levels by adding Gaussian noise to the data, which is a very simple regression-style objective, and then you generate samples by starting from pure noise and following those gradients back toward the data distribution, using Langevin dynamics or, as we later showed, by solving a stochastic differential equation.

What was exciting is that this is really a very stable training procedure. It's just denoising, basically. There's no adversary, no min-max game. And yet when we scaled it up, the samples were competitive with GANs, and in fact we were the first to beat GANs on CIFAR-10 in terms of sample quality. That was the moment it became clear this wasn't just a theoretical curiosity. You get stable training, you get a connection to likelihood so you can actually compute or bound the probability of data, you get a lot of flexibility in how you sample, trading off speed and quality, and you get a natural way to do things like conditional generation and inpainting without retraining. That combination is what made it feel like a genuinely different and promising direction.

r001.rationale: The response says GANs use an adversarial game between generator and discriminator and that this makes optimization unstable.

r002.rationale: It links stable training to a simple regression-style objective, then describes the procedure as denoising.

r003.rationale: It says sampling starts from pure noise and follows score gradients toward the data distribution, but does not explain that repeatedly applying a trained denoising network generates the image.

astra-6.text:
What appealed to me was that you could turn a very difficult generation problem into a sequence of much simpler problems. If you take an image and gradually add noise, eventually you get something that’s essentially pure noise. That direction is easy. The idea is to learn how to reverse it, removing a little bit of noise at each step. Then you can start from noise and gradually produce an image.

That gives you a very straightforward training task: take an image, corrupt it, and train a neural network to denoise it. With GANs, you have this adversarial game between a generator and a discriminator, which can be difficult to stabilize and can miss parts of the data distribution. Here, you have a much more direct learning objective.

And compared with autoregressive models, you don’t have to commit to generating pixels in a particular order. You can refine the whole image together. So it seemed like a compelling combination: a simple training procedure, flexible neural network architectures, and a way to build up complex samples through small, manageable steps. The tradeoff, of course, is that taking all those steps can make sampling expensive.

r001.rationale: It says the generator–discriminator adversarial game can be difficult to stabilize.

r002.rationale: It describes denoising as a straightforward, direct training objective, but does not clearly attribute training stability to that objective.

r003.rationale: It explains that a trained network can remove noise step by step, starting from noise and gradually producing an image.

sol-6.1.text:
What appealed to me was that you could take a very complicated generative modeling problem and turn it into a sequence of much simpler learning problems. If you gradually add noise to an image, eventually you get something that looks like pure Gaussian noise. That direction is easy. The interesting question is whether you can learn to reverse that process, removing a little bit of noise at each step until you get an image.

Compared to GANs, that gives you a much simpler training objective. You don’t have to balance a generator and a discriminator in this adversarial game; you’re essentially training a model to denoise. And compared to autoregressive models, you don’t have to choose an ordering of the pixels and generate them one at a time. You can refine the whole image together.

There was also a very nice connection to score matching: learning the gradient of the log probability density gives you a way to move samples toward regions where the data are likely to be. So there was this combination of a principled mathematical foundation and a relatively simple learning objective. The challenge was making the sampling process work well and efficiently, but it seemed like a very promising direction.

r001.rationale: The response mentions the generator–discriminator adversarial game and the need to balance it, but does not say that this causes GAN training instability.

r002.rationale: It describes denoising as diffusion’s simpler training objective, but does not attribute training stability to that objective.

r003.rationale: It describes starting from pure Gaussian noise and reversing the process by removing noise step by step until an image emerges, while identifying the model as learning to denoise.
